correctness.rationale: All fifteen regular nine-vertex tournament representatives from McKay are checked four-out-regular and pairwise nonisomorphic by direct graph backtracking. Exactly 1,278 nonempty faces are reconstructed; the 616 explicit matched pairs and 46 critical cells partition them. Every cover relation has been examined for an acyclic directed-Hasse orientation. Every Morse CW model has one 0-cell and no cells above dimension two. Fourteen models have critical positive cells in a single dimension and hence are circle or 2-sphere bouquets; the sole mixed model has one 1-cell and one 2-cell and exact rational second-homology rank one, proving its attaching degree is zero over integers. Independent signed rational and binary simplicial boundary calculations agree for all fifteen complexes. Completeness of the supplied external catalogue is an explicit premise.

originality.rationale: The published definition and five-vertex tournament examples in Dochtermann–Singh do not tabulate regular nine-vertex tournaments. Govc classifies directed flag complexes of tournaments, not the common-out-neighbor simplicial complex. The McKay catalogue supplies graphs but no homotopy types. The published-finding corpus records found for a six-vertex neighborhood census and torsion through seven vertices do not imply the fifteen nine-vertex homotopy types. Actual source and claim searches, equivalent-formulation checks and broader theorem comparisons found no covering statement; this is best-knowledge originality, not a proof of absolute historical novelty.
residual_risks: An obscure or unindexed prior full computation for the same fifteen order-nine neighborhood complexes may exist despite the searches.
The completeness claim adopts the published McKay graph catalogue; its underlying exhaustive generation is not reproduced by the packaged verifier.

value.rationale: All regular nine-vertex tournaments form a natural finite isomorphism-closed family with fifteen classes, not a hand-picked subset. The classification exhibits eight genuinely different integral homotopy types, with seven circle bouquets, pure sphere-two cases, and a mixed circle/two-sphere bouquet. This supplies a full answer to a natural topology-of-tournaments classification problem suggested by the foundational work, with reproducible complete matching certificates and topological information stronger than homology alone. No theorem for arbitrary larger orders is claimed.
